    Home/Learn/How to read a peptide COA (certificate of analysis)

    How to read a peptide COA, and what it cannot tell you.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    A COA is a lab report for one batch. It usually shows how pure the peptide is and whether it is the right one; check whether it also covers the amount, bacterial toxins and germs. It tells you about that batch only, and only if a lab outside the shop did the test.

    What is a COA?

    A certificate of analysis, or COA, is a short report from a lab that tested a sample of a product. For peptides it is usually one or two pages with the product name, a batch or lot number, the date of the test, the tests that were run and the results.

    Shops that sell research-use peptides often post COAs on their product pages. A COA is the closest thing these products have to a quality check, because no approved product exists and no regulator checked the vial.1

    Who issues a COA?

    There are two kinds. A third-party COA comes from a lab that the shop does not own. A seller COA is made by the shop or by the factory that made the powder. Only the first kind is an outside check.

    Look for the lab's name, address and a way to check the report, such as a code or link on the lab's own site. A report with no lab name, or one that names the shop as the lab, tells you only what the shop says about itself.

    What does a COA test?

    A full report covers five things. Check which of them your report has:

    • Purity. How much of the powder is the peptide, shown as a percentage (often measured by HPLC). The rest can be leftovers from making it.
    • Identity. Whether the peptide is the one on the label, usually by mass spectrometry: the weight of the molecule found should match the weight expected.
    • Quantity. How many milligrams are really in the vial. A pure peptide in a half-full vial is still not what you paid for.
    • Endotoxin. Toxins left behind by bacteria.
    • Sterility. Whether living germs grew from the sample.

    Many peptide COAs show purity and identity only. A report that lists only purity tells you nothing about the amount, toxins or germs.

    Why does a COA cover only one batch?

    A COA is for the sample the lab received. It is worth something only if the batch or lot number on the report matches the number on your vial. A shop can make a new batch every few weeks; a report from last year says nothing about this month's powder.

    Check the date too. A report much older than the product listing, or the same report on several different products, is a warning sign.

    What does a good COA look like?

    • It names an outside lab, with an address and a way to check the report on the lab's own site.
    • It has a batch or lot number that is also printed on the vial.
    • It is dated, and the date fits the product you are buying.
    • It shows how each result was measured (for example HPLC for purity, mass spectrometry for identity).
    • It covers more than purity: the amount in the vial, and for anything injected, endotoxin and sterility.

    How often do shops publish them?

    A shop with reports is not a shop with good products. It is a shop that shows some of its work.

    What can a COA not tell you?

    It cannot tell you that a peptide is safe or that it works in people. Only trials can show that, and for research-use peptides there are none that the FDA reviewed.2 It cannot tell you a dose, and we do not either.

    Signs that a report needs a closer look: no lab name, no batch number, the same purity to the decimal on every product, a date before the product existed, or a file that looks edited. When in doubt, the lab named on the report can usually confirm whether it issued it.
